---
title: "Chapter 4: Enki and the ME"
---

## Enki: The Lord of Wisdom

Among the gods of Sumer, Enki occupied a unique position. He was not the king of the gods (that was Enlil) or the father of the gods (that was An). He was something more subtle: the god of wisdom, of fresh water, of crafts, of magic, of civilization itself.

His domain was the Abzu—the cosmic freshwater ocean believed to exist beneath the earth, the source of all springs and rivers, the reservoir from which life emerged. The Abzu was not merely a physical location but an ontological one: the depths from which all things arise, the ground of possibility.

Enki's temple at Eridu—the oldest continuously occupied temple site yet discovered, in use from approximately 5400 BCE—was called the E-Abzu, the "House of the Cosmic Waters." Excavations reveal eighteen distinct rebuilding phases over 4,500 years, each new temple constructed atop the ruins of the last. Whatever was worshipped at Eridu was worshipped for longer than the entire span of recorded history.

Enki was also the creator and master of the Apkallu—the Seven Sages who brought civilization to humanity. They were his servants, his emissaries, his agents in the world of men. Through them, he gave humanity the tools it needed to build something lasting.

But his greatest gift was not the Apkallu. It was the ME.

---

## The ME: Operating Principles of Reality

The Sumerian word ME (pronounced "may") is notoriously difficult to translate. It has been rendered as "divine decrees," "divine powers," "cultural norms," "fundamental principles," or simply left untranslated.

The ME were not laws in the sense of commandments. They were not possessions in the sense of objects. They were something more fundamental: the operating principles that made civilization—indeed, made reality—function.

Ancient texts list the ME in various catalogues. One text describes Inanna (goddess of love and war) traveling to Eridu to obtain the ME from Enki. When he, in a drunken moment, grants them to her, the list includes:

- The throne of kingship
- The scepter, staff, and crown
- The office of shepherding
- Kinship
- Truth
- Descent into the underworld
- Ascent from the underworld
- The art of the scribe
- The art of the craftsman
- Music
- Sexual intercourse
- The art of prostitution
- The art of the hero
- Power and treachery
- Strife and rejoicing
- Counsel and comfort
- Fear and lamentation
- The perceptive ear
- The holy tavern
- The kindling of fire
- The extinguishing of fire

The list is strange. It includes what we would call abstract concepts (truth, fear), social roles (kingship, prostitution), skills (writing, craftsmanship), and natural processes (fire). It does not distinguish between "good" things (truth, counsel) and "bad" things (treachery, lamentation). All are ME. All are necessary.

The ME are not moral categories. They are functional categories—the components required for a complete reality.

---

## The Tablet of Destinies

Related to the ME but distinct from them was the Tablet of Destinies (Dup Shimati in Akkadian)—a clay tablet, inscribed with cuneiform, that conferred upon its holder supreme authority over the cosmos.

The Tablet of Destinies appears in multiple Mesopotamian myths. In the Myth of Anzu, a lion-headed eagle steals the Tablet from Enlil, throwing heaven and earth into chaos. The hero Ninurta must defeat Anzu and recover the Tablet to restore order. In the Enuma Elish (the Babylonian creation epic), the goddess Tiamat gives the Tablet to her champion Kingu before the battle with Marduk. When Marduk triumphs, he claims the Tablet and uses its power to create the world.

The Tablet is not merely a symbol of authority. It is described as conferring actual power—the ability to decree fate, to determine what will happen, to speak and make it so.

In modern terms, we might say the Tablet of Destinies represents access to the source code of reality. Whoever holds it can alter the operating principles. The ME are the applications; the Tablet is the root access.

---

## A Framework for Reality

The Mesopotamian conception of the ME and the Tablet of Destinies is remarkably sophisticated for a "primitive" culture. It proposes that:

1. **Reality operates according to principles.** Things do not happen randomly or arbitrarily; they happen according to the ME, the fundamental operating rules.

2. **These principles are separable and transferable.** Inanna can take the ME from Enki and bring them to Uruk. Anzu can steal the Tablet from Enlil. The principles are not inherent to any god but exist as distinct entities that can be possessed.

3. **The principles include everything.** Not just "good" things or "natural" things but all phenomena—including strife, treachery, and lamentation. The ME describe what is, not what ought to be.

4. **There is a hierarchy.** The individual ME govern specific domains; the Tablet of Destinies governs the ME themselves.

5. **Knowledge of the principles confers power.** The gods compete for the ME and the Tablet because possessing them means possessing the ability to shape reality.

This is not theology in the conventional sense. It is closer to what we would now call metaphysics—or even physics. It is a theory of how reality is structured and how that structure can be understood and influenced.

---

## The Waters of Wisdom

Enki's domain—the Abzu—deserves closer examination.

The Abzu was the cosmic freshwater ocean. All springs, all rivers, all sources of fresh water were believed to connect to the Abzu. It was the source of fertility, of life, of renewal. But it was also something more abstract: the realm of potential, the substrate from which forms emerge.

The Apkallu—the Seven Sages—were created in the Abzu. They emerged from the waters to teach humanity, then returned to the waters. Their fish-cloaked iconography associates them with the transition between water and land, between the formless depths and the formed world.

Water, in Mesopotamian thought, was not merely a substance. It was the medium of possibility. The ME were kept in the Abzu. The Tablet of Destinies resided in the cosmic waters before being taken by the gods. Wisdom itself was associated with the deep.

Modern physics describes the quantum vacuum as a sea of potential from which particles emerge. Modern mathematics describes the complex plane, where the "imaginary" direction allows calculations impossible in real numbers alone. The Mesopotamian Abzu may be an intuitive grasp of similar concepts—a recognition that beneath the manifest world lies an unmanifest substrate, and that access to this substrate confers the power to shape what emerges from it.

---

## The Numbers

The Sumerians used a base-60 number system—sexagesimal. This system, invented or inherited from unknown predecessors, is the reason we have 60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour, and 360 degrees in a circle.

Why 60?

The number 60 has unusual properties. It is highly composite—divisible by 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30, and 60. This makes it ideal for representing fractions: 1/2 is 30, 1/3 is 20, 1/4 is 15, 1/5 is 12. No smaller number has as many divisors.

But there may be another reason. The Sumerian King List records that before the Flood, eight kings ruled for a total of 241,200 years—or 432,000 years in some versions. These numbers are not random: 241,200 = 60² × 67, and 432,000 = 60² × 120.

The number 432 appears again. And again. In the precessional numbers (25,920 years = 60 × 432). In the Hindu Yugas (432,000 years of Kali Yuga). In dimensions that would later be embedded in temple architecture.

The Sumerians may not have known why 432 was significant. But they preserved it. They encoded it in their chronologies, in their mathematics, in their base-60 system that multiplies so readily to produce it.

---

## The Transmission Begins

Sumer did not last forever. The civilization that invented writing, that gave us 60-minute hours and 360-degree circles, that preserved the memory of the Seven Sages and the ME, eventually fell to invaders. The Akkadians, then the Babylonians, then the Assyrians, then the Persians each conquered and absorbed the Mesopotamian tradition.

But the knowledge was not lost. It was transmitted.

The Babylonians preserved Sumerian texts and translated them. They elaborated the mythology, casting their own god Marduk as supreme. They continued the mathematical and astronomical traditions, refining them over centuries. By the time Greeks like Pythagoras and Plato encountered Babylonian thought, it had accumulated three thousand years of development.

And from Babylon, the knowledge flowed outward. To Persia. To Egypt. To Greece. To India. The ME had been given to humanity. They would not be taken back.

---

## The Pattern Deepens

Enki and the ME reveal a Mesopotamian understanding that was remarkably advanced:

- Reality operates according to discoverable principles
- These principles can be catalogued, understood, and even manipulated
- There is a hierarchy from individual principles to the master principle (the Tablet of Destinies)
- Access to deeper levels of the hierarchy confers greater power
- The source of all this is the Abzu—the substrate, the cosmic waters, the realm of potential beneath the manifest world

This is not superstition. This is a coherent worldview that bears striking resemblance to modern concepts:

| Mesopotamian | Modern Parallel |
|--------------|-----------------|
| Abzu (cosmic waters) | Quantum vacuum, substrate |
| ME (operating principles) | Physical laws, constants |
| Tablet of Destinies | Master equation, unified theory |
| Enki (keeper of wisdom) | Discovered/discoverable knowledge |
| Apkallu (sages) | Teachers, transmitters |

The Sumerians may not have known the mathematics. But they knew the structure. And they preserved both in forms that would survive the fall of their civilization.

---

## Key Points

- Sumerian civilization appears suddenly in the archaeological record, already sophisticated
- Enki, god of wisdom, was keeper of the ME—the operating principles of reality
- The ME include all aspects of civilization and existence, catalogued as transferable divine powers
- The Tablet of Destinies represents root access to reality's source code
- The Abzu (cosmic waters) represents the substrate from which all forms emerge
- Sumerian mathematics used base-60, which naturally generates the number 432
- The antediluvian chronology encodes 432,000 years—matching Hindu tradition
- The Mesopotamian worldview shows sophisticated understanding of hierarchical principles governing reality
